source.title: Softmax Linear Units
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Neel Nanda; Tom Henighan; Scott Johnston; Sheer El Showk; Nicholas Joseph; Nova DasSarma; Ben Mann; Danny Hernandez; Amanda Askell; Kamal Ndousse; Andy Jones; Dawn Drain; Anna Chen; Yuntao Bai; Deep Ganguli; Liane Lovitt; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; Jackson Kernion; Tom Conerly; Shauna Kravec; Stanislav Fort; Saurav Kadavath; Josh Jacobson; Eli Tran-Johnson; Jared Kaplan; Jack Clark; Tom Brown; Sam McCandlish; Dario Amodei; Christopher Olah

record.file_problem: none; figures (Fig. 1, 2, 4, 9) are not in the text, so per-size values are not available.
record.tranche_reason: It applies the polysemanticity finding to transformer language models and reports an architectural intervention (SoLU) with blinded interpretability rates. It also gives its own caveats on the measure (top-activation examples only) and on superposition. It is one of the original sources, so it is not scored as a test of the versions it originated.
record.gate_note: Not rows: the 30-50% effective-size penalty for SoLU without LayerNorm (stated as preliminary, no numbers per model); the qualitative neuron examples in Section 6.3 (selected examples, no rates); the superposition arguments in Sections 3 and 4 (theory); and the cited prior work on vision neurons.
record.test_reason: The paper takes the polysemanticity question from vision, where the Zoom In original worked, to transformer language models from 1 to 64 layers (up to about 50B parameters). That makes it T3. The config lists it as an original source for V2 and V5, so those versions get no verdict here. Its own results bear on two versions it did not originate. V3: SoLU without the extra LayerNorm made neurons look more interpretable but performed like a model 30-50% smaller (Section 4.3). Adding LayerNorm restored performance, and the low post-LayerNorm activations then became mixed (Section 6.4). The authors call this circumstantial evidence for superposition. V7: one stricter rater marked about 20% of baseline neurons interpretable, against about 40% for the other two (Section 6.2). Also, a neuron that looked clean on its top examples had many unrelated low-activation examples after LayerNorm (Section 6.4).
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right but drops the LayerNorm condition. Corrected version: SoLU with an extra post-activation LayerNorm raises the share of MLP neurons that look interpretable on a 1-2 minute blinded look at top (pre-LayerNorm) examples. The share goes from ~35% to ~60% in 1-40 layer models, and only from 33% to 42% at 64 layers (~50B). Loss stays within a 0.95-1.05x model-size equivalent, and downstream evals show no systematic difference. The 'no cost' result holds only with the LayerNorm: in preliminary runs, SoLU alone performed like a model 30-50% smaller. The LayerNorm appears to let non-neuron-aligned features through as small activations, so SoLU may 'hide' some features. The authors call SoLU a 'double-edged sword' but still a net win, and a proof of concept that architecture can dramatically affect polysemanticity. They read the performance pattern as moderate, 'albeit circumstantial' evidence for superposition. A caveat added after publication says top-example ratings only show whether a neuron is monosemantic when it activates strongly, and are probably a poor guide for architecture experiments.
record.recipe_differences: This is an original source, so it is not compared with an earlier method. It uses a blinded human rating of top dataset examples (80% of top firings explained by one rule) instead of feature visualization.
record.method_sensitivity: The interpretable rate depends on the annotator's strictness (about 20% vs 60% for the strict annotator, against about 40% vs 60% for the others). It depends on model size (64L gain is only 33% to 42%). It depends on the post-activation LayerNorm (the 16L LayerNorm-only model sits about halfway). The authors' later caveat says top examples miss low-activation behaviour, and Figure 9 shows more inconsistent examples at low activations after LayerNorm.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.3.5, anecdotal: some neurons in small SoLU models appear to 'split' into several narrower neurons in larger models. Examples: a hexadecimal neuron splits into neurons for specific hex characters, and a 'German in this context' neuron splits into neurons for specific German tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: As language models grow, a neuron for a broad feature splits into several neurons for narrower sub-features.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 6.3.2-6.3.4, selected examples from SoLU models: early-layer neurons de-tokenize (multi-token words, a token in a specific language), middle-layer neurons carry abstract concepts, and late-layer neurons re-tokenize words into output tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLP neurons in transformer language models change role with depth: early layers map tokens to words, middle layers hold abstract concepts, and late layers map words back to tokens.

record.problems: Raters were authors, with 60 neurons per model and no error bars. The rating uses only top dataset examples, with no negative examples, and the authors later called it a poor guide. The LayerNorm analysis (Figure 9) is a single neuron and not blinded. Per-size results are in figures only. The rating measures first-glance interpretability, not polysemanticity directly. Only one architecture and dataset were tested, and no hyperparameter tuning was done.
record.rows_left_out: Per-size rates in Figure 4 and the downstream task scores in Figure 2 are figure-only and were not turned into rows. The only exception is the 64L numbers, which the text states.

untested.parts: Not tested. The vision polysemantic neuron (cat heads, car fronts, paws) is only cited from prior work (Section 3.3).

There is no direct count of polysemantic neurons; the measure is 'not interpretable at first glance' on top examples, which does not separate polysemantic neurons from neurons uninterpretable for other reasons. The per-layer share is not measured; there is only a qualitative remark that early-layer baseline neurons were especially hard. (Original source; no verdict.)

There is no estimate of how many features the model represents compared with its neurons, and superposition in the baseline model is not measured. The alternatives the paper names (chance misalignment, alien features) are not tested. The SoLU-alone penalty is preliminary, with no per-model numbers and no interpretability rate. LayerNorm was first added for activation-scale and optimization reasons, and that confound is not ruled out.
Not tested. Initialization, regularization and training noise without capacity pressure are not examined.

Only one transformer family and one dataset are tested, with no hyperparameter tuning. Vision models, modern convnets and regularizers are not tested. The LayerNorm-only control exists at 16 layers only. (Original source; no verdict.)
Not tested. The paper only remarks that a deep commonality between cat paws and car fronts can't be ruled out, though it seems less likely.

There is no systematic comparison of scoring rules, the 80% threshold, inspection time or automated explanations. The activation-range check covers one neuron, categorized informally and unblinded (impressions only for others) and SoLU models only; low-activation behaviour of baseline-model neurons is not checked. The rater effect rests on one annotator.

missing.what: SoLU without the extra LayerNorm (preliminary). It 'seemed to make neurons much more interpretable' (no rate given), but performance matched a model 30-50% smaller, with larger models hit harder. This is half of the authors' superposition argument, and a case where lowering polysemanticity costs performance, which V5's 'without a large loss' depends on. The gate_note excludes it as preliminary, but rows_left_out does not declare it and no row records it.

Qualitative layer statement about baseline models: despite significant effort, the authors made almost no progress on early-layer MLP neurons, especially the first MLP layer. In SoLU models many of those neurons were easy to understand. This is the paper's only bearing on V2's 'more in some layers than others', and it says SoLU's effect is especially large in early layers.
missing.locator: Section 2 (overview of feature types); Section 6.3.2; Section 8 first paragraph

record.verdict_notes:
This repairs two attempts that the merge validator refused for listing the same row_id more than once. Now there is one row_fix per row_id, its versions list every version the row is linked to, and the state is for the row's primary non-original version. Per-version nuance is in the problem text.

Originals: the config lists this paper as an original source for V2 and V5, so neither gets a label. States on those links are for reference only.

How the attempts' disagreements were settled:
- R7: both attempts had V7 observed and V3 partial. For V5 they split (cannot_determine vs partial). I used observed (V7 is the primary non-original version) and kept cannot_determine for V5 in the problem text, because R7 has no baseline-model comparison.
- R6: Attempt 1 linked R6 to V3; I did not. Loss parity alone does not measure whether superposition causes polysemanticity. So the V3 label rests on R7 plus the Section 4.3 text (recorded under missing).
- Missing item on early-layer neurons: the attempts tagged it V2+V5 and V2; I used V2, V5, since the text also says SoLU's gain is largest there.

Corrections against the source:
- Attempt 2's V3 reason said low activations were 'mostly unrelated'. The text says 'much more likely' to be unrelated.
- Attempt 1's R4 note called the value figure-only, but the text states 'about halfway' in words.

Rows without fixes: R3, R4 and R6 need none.

Card items moved or rejected:
- The card's fits_no_version item (SoLU hiding features) is now covered by R7's links.
- Excerpt E5 is an Introduction claim, not a result, and its V3/R4 link is wrong.
- The UPDATE, CAVEAT and FOLLOW-UP boxes are later author views (Toy Models, Towards Monosemanticity), not results of this paper.

Other context:
- Figures 1, 2, 4 and 9 are absent from the text, so per-size rates are unavailable except at 64 layers. Section 8 adds that the gain is 'very strong' at 12B, with a sharp transition around 50B.
- Raters were authors, with 60 neurons per model and no error bars.

The text contains no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models are only cited (the cat/car/paw neuron comes from prior work).
Only the share judged not interpretable on top examples is measured; no per-layer rates are given in the text, and no direct count of polysemantic neurons.
No direct test of superposition. The authors call the evidence circumstantial (LayerNorm restores performance, and SoLU reduces interpretable-neuron loss only partly).
Only one transformer family and one dataset were tested. Vision models, modern convnets and regularization were not.
The shift in measurement is shown informally on one neuron, and a stricter annotator is reported. No systematic comparison of scoring methods.

rows.subject: baseline transformer (no SoLU), 1 to 40 layers
rows.operation_detail: blinded human rating of top-activating examples; 60 neurons per model; INTERPRETABLE if a single rule explains 80% of strongest firings
rows.note: Text gives the rate for the 1L-40L group only; per-size values are in the figure. Roughly 65% not interpretable at first glance, which is not the same as polysemantic. The measure uses top examples only.
rows.check: The values are right (~35% interpretable, 1-40 layers). Section 6.2 adds that the 64-layer baseline rate is about the same (33%), so the subject can extend to 1-64 layers. The ~65% 'not interpretable at first glance' is not a direct polysemanticity count: it mixes polysemantic neurons with otherwise hard-to-read ones (a rule not found in 1-2 minutes, possible alien features), and neurons rated interpretable may still be polysemantic outside their top examples (Sections 6.1, 6.4). The text gives no per-layer split. For V5 this row is just R2's baseline. Both linked versions are originated here, so the state is for reference only.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2 (~35% for 1-40 layers); Section 6.1 (60 neurons, 1-2 min)

rows.subject: SoLU transformer (with extra LayerNorm), 1 to 40 layers
rows.operation_detail: replace MLP activation with SoLU(x)=x*softmax(x) plus LayerNorm; same blinded rating
rows.uncertainty: not stated numerically; authors cite sample size and consistent gap
rows.note: Raters were authors, blinded to the model.
rows.check: The values are right. The rated activations are top examples of pre-LayerNorm activations only (footnote 2), where SoLU suppresses small activations. See R7 for what appears in low post-LayerNorm activations. Part of the gain may come from the extra LayerNorm rather than SoLU: the 16-layer LayerNorm-only control (R4) sits about halfway. V5 is originated here, so the state is for reference only.

rows.subject: SoLU transformer, 64 layers (50B parameters)
rows.operation_detail: SoLU plus LayerNorm vs baseline, blinded rating
rows.note: The gain is much smaller at 64L. The authors do not know why. They suggest larger models have more sophisticated concepts that are harder to see in 1-2 minutes.

rows.subject: 16-layer model with extra LayerNorm but no SoLU
rows.operation_detail: extra LayerNorm only, to separate the effect of SoLU from the effect of LayerNorm
rows.value: about halfway between SoLU and baseline
rows.note: The authors read this as the LayerNorm alone giving some but not all of the benefit. No exact number in the text.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.2: about halfway between SoLU and baseline; Figure 4 green dot

rows.subject: one stricter annotator, baseline vs SoLU
rows.operation_detail: same blinded rating by the annotator who held a higher bar and was less willing to ignore small activations
rows.measure: fraction of neurons marked interpretable, baseline vs SoLU
rows.value: ~60% (SoLU); the other two annotators gave ~40% vs ~60%
rows.note: Shows that the size of the gap depends on how strict the judge is. The authors hesitate to draw strong inferences.
rows.check: The row records baseline vs SoLU for the strict annotator (~20% vs ~60%). For V7 the relevant contrast is between annotators on baseline neurons: ~20% for the strict annotator, ~40% for the other two. All three rated SoLU at ~60%, so the strictness effect shows on baseline neurons only. The explanation (a higher bar, 'less willing to ignore small activations') comes from conversations after unblinding, and the authors hesitate to infer much from it. This is one of three raters, and the text doesn't say which model sizes the per-annotator rates pool. For V5 (originated here, no verdict) observed also holds: the SoLU gain is larger under the strict annotator.

source_check.problem: Strictness is the authors' post-hoc impression, not a measured condition.

rows.subject: SoLU vs baseline transformers, 1 layer to 64 layers
rows.operation_detail: loss and downstream tasks (Lambada, ARC, OpenBookQA, TriviaQA, arithmetic, MMLU, HellaSwag) for SoLU vs baseline
rows.value: between 0.95x and 1.05x; about +-0.01 nats against total loss of 1.6-3 nats; 1.01x at 50B
rows.uncertainty: authors say differences are more likely than not random noise
rows.note: Downstream: arithmetic better with SoLU, TriviaQA better with baseline, no systematic trend (Figure 2). No hyperparameter tuning for either model.

rows.subject: SoLU model, one neuron (left/right body-part neuron)
rows.operation_detail: one author sorted about 1,000 dataset examples pre- and post-LayerNorm as consistent or inconsistent with the neuron's hypothesis, across activation levels
rows.measure: fraction of examples inconsistent with the primary hypothesis
rows.value: figure only; text says post-LayerNorm examples were much more likely to be unrelated at low activations
rows.note: Suggests a neuron that looks interpretable on top examples can look mixed when low activations are examined.
rows.check: The value is readable from the text and not figure-only: post-LayerNorm activations were 'much more likely to have unrelated activations in the low-activation regime'. Caveats: one SoLU neuron (left/right, body parts), about 1,000 examples, categorized by one author, not blinded. Section 6.4 reports the same impression across 'a variety of neurons'. The baseline should read: pre-LayerNorm examples and high-activation examples. The state given is for V7, the row's primary non-original version. V3 link added, state partial: hidden non-neuron-aligned content in small post-LayerNorm activations is the signature the authors expect from superposition. It does not show that features outnumber neurons, or that superposition causes the baseline's polysemanticity. V5 (originated here, no verdict), state cannot_determine: there is no baseline-model comparison, so the row cannot show a share changing. It only suggests that part of R2's gain is apparent.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6.4, Figure 9: post-LayerNorm low-activation examples more often unrelated; informal, not blinded

relationships.condition: SoLU vs baseline transformer language models: preliminary SoLU-only runs (sizes unstated) plus one SoLU+LayerNorm neuron. Indirect evidence, which the authors call circumstantial.
relationships.reason: This verdict rests partly on text that is not a row (Section 4.3; see missing): SoLU alone made neurons look much more interpretable but performed like a model 30-50% smaller. R7: once LayerNorm restored performance, low post-LayerNorm activations of a neuron that looked clean were much more often unrelated (one neuron, not blinded). A LayerNorm optimization confound is not excluded.
relationships.display_finding: SoLU alone made neurons look much more interpretable but performed like a model 30–50% smaller. Once LayerNorm restored performance, low activations of a clean-looking neuron were much more often unrelated; this was one neuron, not blinded, and a LayerNorm optimization confound is not ruled out.

relation.reason: Its own experiments bear directly on the versions.

tranche.reason: It moves the question to a new setting (transformer LMs) and reports results on the claim. It is an original source for V2/V5, but its V3 and V7 evidence comes from a test in this new setting.

source_check.notes: All 7 rows and both verdicts check out. Ratings were done by the authors, 1-2 minutes per neuron, on top pre-LN examples only, and a later caveat says this shows monosemanticity only for strong activations. The 1L-40L group includes a ~12B model with a 'very strong gain' (Discussion), so 64L is not the only model above 1B. The reading list's 'Baseline only' means no V2/V5 verdicts; the record does carry V3 and V7 supports.

statements.correction: Section 6.2: one annotator ~20% (baseline) vs ~60% (SoLU); the other two ~40% vs ~60%. After unblinding, the authors' sense was that this annotator held a higher bar and was less willing to ignore small activations. They 'hesitate to draw too strong an inference'. Row: R5.
statements.problem: The number pairs have no labels (they are baseline vs SoLU), and raters differ only on baseline neurons. Strictness is the authors' hedged impression after unblinding but is stated as fact. The numbers are in R5, not the cited R1.

statements.correction: Original trains models from 1L to 64L (~50B) in steps of about 4x in parameters. It rates interpretability at 1L, 16L, 24L, 40L and 64L. SoLU gain: 42% vs 33% at 50B (Section 6.2); 'a very strong gain at 12 billion parameters' (Discussion). Section 6 maps only 64L to a size; the 12B model is most likely the 40L.
statements.problem: It implies the original's only model above 1B is the 64L (50B) one. The Discussion also reports a 'very strong gain at 12 billion parameters', so the 1L-40L group (~35% to ~60%) includes a model above 1B.
